title: The sentence of death (2 Corinthians 1:8–11)
hook: Paul despaired even of life, and learned to trust the God who raises the dead
tomorrow: how can one smell mean life to one person and death to another?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: all things with charity, every rule set under love. Now a new letter to the same church, and it opens on Paul's worst season.

A hospital hallway. A plastic chair, a vending machine humming, a door that hasn't opened in an hour. You've already run the worst version in your head three times. Paul put a season like that into a letter. "We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." He names the place, Asia, and stops there. He never says what happened. Then he says something stranger: he'd already heard the verdict.
screen: `A PLASTIC CHAIR, A HUMMING MACHINE.` → `WE DESPAIRED EVEN OF LIFE.` → `THE VERDICT WAS IN.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead." A sentence, like a verdict read out in court. Paul felt it was already in. And he says the verdict did something: it moved his trust off himself. Notice which name for God he reaches for. Not the God who helps the strong get stronger. The God who raises the dead. When you're at the bottom, that's the help that reaches that far down. Then three tenses in one breath. God "delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us." Past, present, future. Then Paul pulls the readers into it: "Ye also helping together by prayer for us." Their prayers, he says, are part of how he's carried, and many will give thanks when he comes through. One to tell a friend tonight: a few verses earlier Paul calls God "the God of all comfort," and in this letter comfort doesn't skip the despair. It arrives inside it, and it arrives with other people.
screen: `THE SENTENCE OF DEATH IN OURSELVES.` · `GOD WHICH RAISETH THE DEAD.` · `DELIVERED, DOTH DELIVER, WILL YET.` · `HELPING TOGETHER BY PRAYER.` · then, large: `THE GOD WHO RAISES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one heavy thing sit in your lap, without trying to solve it. Breathe with it there; if you pray, you can hand it to the God who raises the dead, and think of one person you could ask to carry it with you. If heaviness ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number, right away.
The sentence of death. Paul's word for a verdict he felt was already in, which turned his trust toward the God who raises the dead.
Your line: the God who raises, the name Paul reached for at the very bottom. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians pray for one another in illness and danger, sometimes by name in church, and some turn to 2 Corinthians 1 in a hard season because Paul admits his own despair.

fork.setup: your coach's son is in the hospital, and the team wants to do something. what does Paul's passage point to?
options: send word, show up, and if you pray, pray for him together.
stay away and give the family privacy until it's all over.
tell the coach that everything happens for a good reason.
fork.reveal: ye also helping together by prayer for us. in Paul's letter, comfort arrives inside the trouble, and it arrives with other people.

original.note: Greek: a verdict or official decision, the 'sentence' of 2 Corinthians 1:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was a hero who never cracked.
what it means: Paul despaired even of life, and the verdict he felt moved his trust to the God who raises the dead.
what a scholar hears: apokrima, an official verdict, then three tenses of deliver in one verse (1:10): delivered, doth deliver, will yet deliver.
guess: a verdict that turned trust to God
a court ruling that ended Paul's life
a death penalty Paul gave to others
recall: Let all be done in love

chat.says: pop fell on the porch steps last night. they're keeping him for tests. i can't stop shaking.
options: I'm so sorry. Paul despaired too, and let people carry him in prayer. Can I pray for Pop with you?
Don't worry. God never gives anyone more than they can handle, so Pop will be totally fine.
Stay strong and keep it to yourself, so your dad doesn't have one more person to worry about.
chat.meaning: Paul despaired even of life, trusted the God who raises the dead, and said others' prayers helped carry him. No promise about the outcome; company inside it.

Asia.meaning: here, a Roman province, not the whole continent

pressed out of measure.meaning: crushed far beyond what could be borne
